old_title: Ukraine war live: Putin strikes Kyiv as Zelensky prepares UN address
new_title: Ukraine war live: Trump condemned over Putin G20 invite as CIA issues Russia warning

Russia pounded Kyiv with drone strikes on Wednesday, hitting railway infrastructure, warehouses and fuel stations as Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky prepared to address the UN.
At least two people were killed and 22 injured in the morning attack in one of the heaviest strikes since Russia began attacking Kyiv and nearby areas over the summer with rapid high-flying jet drones.
The strikes came hours after Zelensky met with US president Donald Trump to discuss peace efforts, including hopes of a bilateral ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
On the sidelines of the UN general assembly in New York, Zelensky told the Wall Street Journal on Tuesday that he had asked Trump for a "winter package" of new military equipment and believes the US will push for a deal to stop attacks on energy.
Zelensky said he was ready to meet Russian president Vladimir Putin at a trilateral meeting with president Trump. But the Kremlin signalled on Wednesday its position was unchanged ahead of a meeting between top US and Russian officials in New York.
"For now, there are no prerequisites for moving onto a peaceful negotiating track, although we, as the Russian side, remain open to peace talks," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
Russia attacks port infrastructure in Ukraine's Odesa region
Russia attacked port and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine's southern Black Sea region of Odesa, the regional governor said on Wednesday.
Moscow also hit warehouses used to store medicines, household goods and food, Oleh Kiper said on Telegram.
Kremlin accuses Burnham of stoking anti-Russian sentiment, says no plans for peace talks with Ukraine
On the heels of Andy Burnham's comments to the UN general assembly on Tuesday, the Kremlin has accused the British prime minister of stoking 'anti-Russian sentiment'.
The PM accused Russia of exploiting Brexit to sow division in the UK as he announced a new unit to tackle online disinformation.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Burnham's approach, and that of other European countries, was flawed.
"Well, the British Prime Minister said nothing new. That is the first point. The second is that stoking anti-Russian sentiment and fostering an atmosphere of total Russophobia is what Britain is doing. And now, presumably in unison with Britain, the Germans, the French and a number of other European states are doing the same thing," said Peskov.
"From our point of view, this is an utterly short-sighted policy. It in no way brings us any closer to any steps that might, in the long term, lead to a reduction in tensions and de-escalation on the European continent."
With Volodymyr Zelensky in New York to discuss a potential ceasefire on energy infrastructure with the Trump administration, Peskov also assessed that the groups for wider Ukraine peace talks were still not in place.
He said there were no concrete details on plans to hold any high-level meeting on Ukraine, and that Zelensky would have to come to Moscow for future talks. Zelensky has previously ruled out such a trip.
Senior Nato commander warns Putin is becoming more cavalier and open to risk as Ukraine war drags on
Russian President Vladimir Putin is becoming "increasingly cavalier, dangerous and risk accepting," as his war in Ukraine drags on and as he seeks to divide Western allies, Nato's deputy commander in Europe said Tuesday.
Air Chief Marshal Sir John Stringer spoke at a security conference in Estonia amid warnings from some European leaders that Moscow is planning to test Nato's collective defense pact with bolder attacks that have already included sabotage and espionage.
Stringer warned that Nato members need to be aware of the "febrile environment" and careful in their response because Putin would like to provoke the alliance into an "overreaction."
The UK government wants families to stock up on food. Here's what to buy
UK households are being urged to stock up on essential items in case of emergencies, according to reports.
A new public information drive is set to encourage people to prepare for extreme weather, cyber attacks and hostile state action.
The national resilience campaign aims to highlight the steps people can take to stay safe in a crisis that may cause power or water supplies to stop or where shops are forced to close.
In full:
Preview: Marco Rubio to meet Russian counterpart on Wednesday
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will meet Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov in New York City on Wednesday morning.
The meeting comes after Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky met with US president Donald Trump at the UN headquarters on Tuesday.
Zelensky said he discussed efforts to end the war in Ukraine, including a potential bilateral ceasefire on energy-related targets.
Lavrov is now expected to address the UN general assembly on Saturday.
He said last week that Russia will not stop fighting in Ukraine while any potential talks take place.
NEW: Russian attack on foreign-flagged vessel in Black Sea kills one, Ukraine says
Russia attacked a cargo vessel sailing under the Antigua and Barbuda flag in the Black Sea overnight, killing the captain, Ukraine's seaports authority said on Wednesday.
The attack had caused a fire which was doused and the crew had been evacuated, it said on the Telegram messaging app.
Azerbaijan pardons Frenchman Martin Ryan after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire Usmanov
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev pardoned a French national imprisoned for espionage on Wednesday, a day after the EU lifted sanctions on Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov following what diplomats said was pressure from Baku.
The Frenchman, Martin Ryan, had been serving a ten-year prison sentence in Baku following a conviction in March.
Three European diplomats told Reuters that Paris had indicated in private that Baku was using Usmanov to pressure it over the case of two French citizens held in Azerbaijan, an assertion rejected by Baku.
Latvian PM says removing sanctions on Russian oligarchs means 'normalising Russia'
Latvia initially blocked an EU deal to remove Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the bloc's sanctions list, arguing that delisting individuals in exchange for political or prisoner-release deals could set a dangerous precedent.
Latvian PM Andris Kulbergs told Euronews: "Either it is sports, what we've seen, either culture, and now one by one cherry-picking out of sanctions, that is not the way to go.
"That is normalising Russia."
"I'm worried about the playbook which it leaves," he said.
"I don't think this is a very good example, because that gives a message. 'Oh, we arrest some politicians somewhere, and then we can ask for a sanctions package.' This is not a good playbook, and that's exactly why we froze it for 36 months. That's it. No discussion."
Latvia initially opposed the move but agreed to abstain after securing concessions from France, including talks on French nuclear deterrence cooperation and a stronger French military presence in Latvia.
"It's important for the eastern flank, for us, to have the coverage of their security," he said.
Russia is using Ukrainian POWs to fuel its propaganda - report
Russia has coerced thousands of Ukrainian prisoners of war (POWs) into appearing in propaganda videos, often making them criticise Ukraine or say they do not want to return home, an investigation by NBC has found.
Former POWs told the American broadcaster they were beaten, tortured or threatened, while some cooperated simply to prove they were alive.
The investigation focuses on Ukrainian soldier Volodymyr Srebrodolskyy, whose 2024 propaganda video led people in his home village to believe he had betrayed Ukraine.
He later died in Russian captivity, and some villagers opposed burying him locally. His cousin said: "At least they could have buried him near his mother."
Former POW Yevhen Shybalov described the propaganda operation as an organised system. "Russian propaganda - it's an industry."
The UN, which interviewed more than 850 Ukrainian POWs, found 96 per cent reported torture or mistreatment, including beatings, electric shocks, sleep deprivation and mock executions.

Donald Trump is facing backlash after inviting Russian president Vladimir Putin to a December G20 meeting in Miami, for what would be his second US visit since the war began.
"It's clearly, I think, the wrong path to normalise people who are starting wars, who are going against the UN charter, who are killing and giving orders to kill civilians," said the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, speaking to Sky News.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio said on Wednesday it would be an opportunity for Putin to engage with other world leaders and that the US hopes he will accepted.
The Kremlin said Russia was "grateful and appreciative" for the invitation and will "make a decision".
It comes after a report in El Mundo that the CIA has warned of a Russian plan to attack Spain, France or Italy using sea drones.
European foreign ministries were issued a detailed report from the agency after CIA Director John Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow.
Concerns are growing that Putin could seek to ramp up Russia's targeting of Nato countries in Europe as it looks to prod the western alliance's defences.
CIA warns Russia planning to attack Spain, France or Italy - report
The CIA has warned European governments of Russian plans to attack Spain, France or Italy using sea drones, according to a report in Spanish outlet El Mundo.
Foreign ministries in the three countries were warned in a report that followed CIA director John Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow
A source told the newspaper: "They will use drones launched from the sea, concealed in a container on a ship. It is not difficult at all."
France, Spain and Italy are being targeted because they are holding elections next year, the report said, with Moscow potentially looking to sow political division as right-wing political forces, that are softer in their stance towards Russia, surge.
The attacks would not be designed to cause major damage, but instead to disrupt logistics,such as by shutting down and airport, or to demonstrate weaknesses in Europe's defences far from the Russian border, says El Mundo.
Moscow has repeatedly stated that European countries assisting Ukraine by providing weapons are legitimate targets of Russian attack.
US and Indian top diplomats discuss Russia sanctions bill signed by Trump
US secretary of state Marco Rubio and Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar discussed on Wednesday US measures that could be leveled against countries that engage economically with Russia and Iran.
Last week, Trump signed the bill called "Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," named after deceased South Carolina Republican US Senator Lindsey Graham.
Rubio and Jaishankar "discussed sanctions that could be leveled against states that engage economically with Russia and Iran," the State Department said in a statement after their meeting in New York.
Jaishankar wrote on X he "reiterated India's interests and concerns with regard to SRIA."
India has previously told Washington that new measures to levy tariffs over the purchase of Russian oil could impact bilateral ties.
Poland suspects Russia behind fire at Starlink satellite station
A fire broke out on Wednesday evening at a ground-based Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland providing connectivity for the region, including Ukraine, deputy prime minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said.
He added that the systems were now operational.
Poland has been on heightened alert for acts of sabotage since Russia's invasion of neighbouring Ukraine in 2022. Russia has repeatedly denied any such action.
"The fire engulfed the power station and the generator; it is clear that this act of sabotage was deliberately designed to disable the station - effectively cutting off the internet connection... and disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian military," he said.
"While everything is operational today, we must recognise -as Prime Minister Tusk recently noted - that this is an element of hybrid warfare."
He added that while it was not established that Russia was responsible for the fire, "many signs suggest this aligns with Russia's new doctrine of attack".
Two North Korean soldiers captured by Ukraine sent to South Korea, Zelensky says
Ukraine has transferred two North Korean soldiers captured while fighting for Russia to South Korea, Volodymyr Zelensky said in an address to the United Nations General Assembly.
"Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea," the Ukrainian president said, revealing that the prisoners had left Ukrainian custody.
South Korea stopped short of publicly confirming the transfer.
"It is difficult to confirm whether the individuals have been handled, the timing and route, or the specific details about the consultations between the two countries," a foreign ministry official said, citing the issue of their safety.
Maroosha Muzaffar writes:
Czech air force says fighter jets were scrambled over Poland
Czech air force JAS-39 Gripen fighter jets were scrambled overnight for combat air patrol over Poland, the Czech army said on Thursday.
The army said on X that there was no need to use force during the mission and the jets have returned to their home base.
Six killed in Russian attack on farm in Kharkiv region
Six people have been killed in a Russian attack on a farm in Ukraine's northern Kharkiv region early on Thursday, the region's governor has said.
Another 12 people were injured in the attack, according to authorities.
"Two men and four women have been killed," Oleh Syniehubov, head of Kharkiv regional military administration, said earlier on Telegram. "We currently know of eight people who have been injured - they are farm workers."
He later revised the injury toll to 12.
Watch: Don't weaken sanctions on Russian oligarchs, Zelensky pleads with world leaders
German minister called for ceasefire starting around the Black Sea
German foreign minister Johann Wadephul called for a full and immediate ceasefire in Ukraine, starting in the Black Sea, to safeguard grain and food supplies.
"Ukraine had a very good grain harvest this year. But because of the Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports, it can't be delivered to the world.
"Russia is thereby exacerbating hunger and starvation worldwide," he said in a statement published on Thursday.
Kremlin accuses Andy Burnham of 'stoking anti-Russian sentiment' in UN speech
Moscow has rebuked prime minister Andy Burnham over a UN General Assembly speech in which he accused Russia of spreading falsehoods, arguing that his comments will do nothing to ease tensions across Europe.
Addressing the summit on Tuesday, Burnham announced London would establish a new National Centre for Information Defence, singling out Moscow over what he termed disinformation.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov characterised the approach taken by Burnham and other European nations as fundamentally flawed.
"Well, the British prime minister said nothing new. That is the first point. The second is that stoking anti-Russian sentiment and fostering an atmosphere of total Russophobia is what Britain is doing. And now, presumably in unison with Britain, the Germans, the French and a number of other European states are doing the same thing," said Peskov.
"From our point of view, this is an utterly short-sighted policy. It in no way brings us any closer to any steps that might, in the long term, lead to a reduction in tensions and de-escalation on the European continent."
The prime minister unveiled plans for a new National Centre for Information Defence to tackle Russian information warfare as he addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Russia has previously been accused of using illicitly acquired documents about UK-US trade talks to try to influence the 2019 contest.
The new unit is initially being led out of the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet, with the new centre working alongside intelligence agencies, government departments, the police and social media companies.
He told world leaders that the UK and its allies had been subjected to an "industrial-scale assault" by hostile states, including Russia, to "prey on people's fear".
The prime minister said misinformation had worsened in recent years, accusing Vladimir Putin's agencies of interfering with the 2019 general election and falsifying newspaper articles.
"It is now ten years since Brexit, my country has lived through the destruction, and it has given us a unique perspective that I want to share with you today," he told the UN.
He added: "In recent years we have seen an industrial-scale assault by hostile actors on the information environment in the UK and many of our allies. Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fears.
"I know this is a shared challenge. So we are going to use our experience in the UK - and the fact that we have already been through this shock - to help other countries."
